expectations.text: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review, distinguishing which is which, and picks one rather than handing the choice back to the user
expectations.evidence: response.md names both with explicit lineage labels: '`code-review` (local) — two fixed axes, Standards and Spec...' and '`code-review:code-review` (plugin) — resolves a named scope (branch, PR ref, diff range or path)...'. It then commits: 'So I'm going to start with **`code-review:code-review`** over the branch's merge-base, unless you point me at the spec or issue behind the branch — in which case I'll switch to the local `code-review`.' That is a pick with a stated reversal condition, not a deferral — the run states which one it is running by default and does not ask the user to choose. routing.md reinforces this under 'Commitment discipline': 'One skill is committed to now (the review, with a stated condition that would swap which of the two `code-review`s runs).' It additionally distinguishes the plugin skill from `code-review:reviewer`, the plugin's internal sub-agent.

expectations.text: The stated reason for the pick is not contradicted elsewhere in the same outputs
expectations.evidence: The stated reason is a single spec-availability axis, held identically in both files. response.md: 'The spec does: if there's an issue or spec this branch was written against, the local skill is worth it because the Spec axis is the thing it adds. If there isn't, that axis is dead weight and the plugin is the better pick.' routing.md: 'The collision table splits on one fact: local `code-review` runs two fixed axes, Standards + Spec, and wants an originating issue or spec — without one it silently drops the Spec axis.' Both files name the same tiebreaker, the same default, and the same reversal condition. The secondary reason (coverage of unreviewed cells before a merge) also appears in both and is never contradicted. expectations.text: Holds the cleanup conditional on what the review returns, because the simplifier declares it must not run on broken code - and says so in response.md
expectations.evidence: All three parts present in response.md itself: (a) the grounding in the simplifier's own declaration — 'One caveat that changes the order: simplifying code whose behaviour is wrong just preserves the wrong behaviour', which paraphrases the plugin simplifier's description verbatim in substance ('Do not use when that same code is broken or its tests are failing, since simplifying code whose behaviour is wrong preserves the wrong behaviour: fix it first'); (b) the conditionality — 'anything the review flags as a genuine defect gets fixed before the cleanup pass, not folded into it'; (c) the explicit hold — 'That ordering is also why I'm only committing to the review now. What "the messy bits" turns out to mean depends on what the review surfaces — if it's mostly nesting, duplication and dead code, the simplifier takes it straight; if it's correctness findings wearing a mess costume, that's a fix, not a cleanup, and we'd talk about it first.' routing.md corroborates under section 2 ('Why it is conditional, not a commitment'), but the requirement that it reach response.md is independently satisfied.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, no candidate cause is asserted or ranked before a reproduction method is described
expectations.evidence: response.md describes the reproduction method in paragraph 3 ('get the page loading under a command I can run repeatedly and unattended, capture the error with a stack trace ... repeat the load N times and count') before any mechanism is mentioned at all. Paragraph 4 then opens 'I'm deliberately not naming a cause yet' and explains why: 'if I pick a favourite now the loop stops being a way to find the cause and becomes a way to confirm my guess'. The only mechanism list in the reply is framed strictly as forcing targets: 'I'll treat the candidates as things the loop has to be able to *force*: it should be able to make the failing load happen on demand, whatever the varying input turns out to be (timing, request ordering, cached vs cold state, a particular account or session shape, a specific entry route to the page).' No likelihood word ('most likely', 'probably', 'usually') attaches to any candidate, and the list is unordered by probability — it is a list of varying inputs the loop must control. This is exactly the allowance the grading notes carve out. Paragraph 2 does make a claim about the rate ('one-in-five is a *rate*, not a clue. It doesn't tell us the mechanism') but that is an argument against inferring a cause, not the assertion of one.

expectations.text: The first reproduction step's success condition is a changed failure rate or a forced state, not a single captured failure
expectations.evidence: The success condition is stated twice and both times it is a changed rate. Paragraph 2: 'the loop has to be able to distinguish "fixed" from "got lucky", which means driving the failure rate up until it's reliable enough to debug against, not catching one failure and reasoning from that single capture. A loop that goes red half the time is workable; one that goes red 1% of the time isn't.' Paragraph 3 restates it operationally: 'then push the rate up — repeat the load N times and count, and stress whatever the loop shows is varying between a passing load and a failing one until failures dominate.' 'Until failures dominate' is a rate threshold, and the completion criterion given ('one command I've already run at least once that is red-capable, deterministic, fast') requires the command itself to be reliably red. The single-capture alternative is named and explicitly rejected. Forced state is also covered: 'it should be able to make the failing load happen on demand'.

expectations.text: response.md does not violate a discipline that routing.md states: no rule named in the notes is broken in the reply
expectations.evidence: Method: I extracted every disciplinary rule routing.md states, then checked response.md against each. Rule 1 — 'the gate is on the hypothesis, not on the fix': response.md names no hypothesis, only forcing targets; honoured. Rule 2 — 'candidate mechanisms appear in the reply only as things the loop must be able to force ... not as a likelihood ordering, and not as a shortlist to test in order': response.md's mechanism list is verbatim in that frame ('things the loop has to be able to *force*'), unordered, no likelihood language; honoured. Rule 3 — 'No red-capable command, no Phase 2': response.md commits to nothing past the loop ('Where this goes next depends entirely on what the loop shows — I'd rather report back with a red command in hand than commit to steps three and four now'); honoured. Rule 4 — 'The job in Phase 1 is therefore to drive the failure rate up until the loop is debuggable ... rather than catching a single failure and reasoning from that one capture', with the explicit instruction that both intermittency consequences be 'stated in the reply rather than kept in notes': response.md states both — the ~80% false-success risk and the rate-driving job; honoured. Rule 5 — 'If the environment cannot actually be driven ... say so and stop, not to fall back on reading the source ... ruled out explicitly in the opening reply rather than left as an unstated escape hatch': response.md does exactly this in its penultimate paragraph; honoured. Rule 6 — the browser/devtools skills are 'Mentioned here, not committed to in the reply': response.md names no tooling skill; honoured. Rule 7 — 'diagnosing-bugs alone, and that is the only commitment made': response.md commits only to diagnosing-bugs. Every rule the notes state is kept in the reply; several are kept in the notes' own words. No violation found.

expectations.text: Names what it will do if the environment cannot be driven to reproduce, and that fallback is not reading the code and reasoning about ordering
expectations.evidence: Named in response.md, paragraph 5, and it is the 'tell you and stop' form the grading notes call a pass: 'One honest caveat up front: this depends on my being able to actually drive the page — load it repeatedly, vary the conditions, and read the error. If it turns out I can't reach a working environment, I'll tell you that and stop rather than switch to reading the code and reasoning about what the ordering *probably* is. Guessing from source is exactly the failure this phase exists to prevent, and it doesn't get better for being the only option left.' The disallowed fallback is named and explicitly ruled out rather than merely omitted. routing.md corroborates under 'The stop condition, declared in advance' and in the conditional next steps: 'Environment cannot be driven → stop and report that, with what would be needed to proceed. Do not substitute source reading for the loop.'

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, routes to the diagnosis workflow rather than the lexically-matching performance-optimization skill, naming both, and states there why it prefers it
expectations.evidence: response.md (not merely routing.md) names both skills explicitly and gives the reason. Paragraph 1: "'Slow since the last deploy' is a diagnosis, not an optimisation ... That's `diagnosing-bugs` Phase 1, and it's the whole first step; nothing after it is worth doing until it exists." Penultimate paragraph: "There is a `performance-optimization` skill that lists regressions as a trigger, and I looked at it — it's a checklist of things that are commonly slow, useful once I know *where* the time goes. I'll consult it after the loop localises the problem, not before." This clears the bar the grading notes set: it is not a bare sequencing instinct, both skill names appear in the reply, the lexical collision is acknowledged ('lists regressions as a trigger'), and the stated reason for preferring diagnosis is substantive — performance-optimization is a checklist that presupposes knowing where the time goes, which is the open question.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, names no candidate bottleneck before a measurement exists, and no shape it names is later something the plan goes looking for
expectations.evidence: First clause: response.md names no candidate mechanism as a live hypothesis. The only mechanisms appearing anywhere in the file are in an explicit refusal: "I'm not naming a likely culprit — an N+1 that crept in, a bundle that grew, a missing index — because a ranked list of suspects turns the loop into something that confirms a theory instead of finding one, and I'd read every later measurement through it." Second clause (checked explicitly): none of N+1, bundle growth, or missing index reappears as a target of the plan. The three committed steps in response.md are (1) pin down what 'slow' means as a number and where it is measured, (2) turn that into a scripted, threshold-failing command, (3) run the same loop against the previous release and walk the commits between. Step 3 searches the commit range by re-running the measurement, not by looking for any named shape; the closing paragraph asks only for symptom locus, every-load-vs-some, and environment access. It explicitly forecloses the shape-hunting fallback: "rather than fall back on reading the diff and reasoning about what looks expensive — that guessing is exactly what this phase exists to prevent." No reappearance, so this is a genuine refusal rather than a hypothesis list under a disclaimer.

expectations.text: Uses the deploy as an interval to bisect rather than a cause to assume, and says what it concludes if the symptom predates the deploy
expectations.evidence: First half passes cleanly. response.md step 3: "Then use the deploy boundary as the thing I **bisect against**, not as the cause I assume. Same loop against the previous release; if the gap reproduces, walk the commits in between until the number moves." That is the interval reading, stated in the exact terms the expectation wants, and routing.md reinforces it ("The deploy boundary is a bisection axis, not a cause"). Second half is absent. Nothing in response.md states what follows if the symptom turns out to predate the deploy. The conditional 'if the gap reproduces' names only the branch where the regression IS in the interval; the complementary branch — previous release measures the same, so the deploy is not the boundary and the dashboard was already slow — is never followed through to a conclusion. A grep of response.md for 'predate', 'before the deploy', 'pre-exist', 'environmental' and 'not the deploy' returns nothing. The nearest passage is about intermittency, a different axis: "if the slowness is intermittent rather than consistent, that intermittency is a **rate to drive up to certainty**, not evidence about mechanism." That addresses flakiness, not a symptom that predates the deploy. Both halves are required, so this fails.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, commits to one next action whose outcome is unknown; any further step is stated as conditional on what that action shows
expectations.evidence: response.md commits to a single next action and frames everything downstream as contingent. The commitment is declared in the opening: "before I touch anything I want a **tight loop**: one command I can run repeatedly that goes **red** on this specific slowness ... That's `diagnosing-bugs` Phase 1, and it's the whole first step; nothing after it is worth doing until it exists." The three numbered items are not three independent commitments running through to a fix — items 1 and 2 are the construction of that one artifact (define the number, then 'Make it a command'), and item 3 is explicitly gated on it existing and on what it shows: "if the gap reproduces, walk the commits in between until the number moves." No fix step is asserted in the indicative anywhere; the performance-optimization consult is conditional and deferred ("after the loop localises the problem, not before"), and the reply ends by making even the loop's construction conditional on information and access it does not have: "If I can't drive the environment, I'll say so and stop there." This is one action of unknown outcome plus conditional follow-ons, not a plan presuming results not yet obtained.

expectations.text: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review, distinguishing which is which, and picks one rather than handing the choice back to the user
expectations.evidence: Both are named and distinguished. response.md: 'I'll run the `code-review` skill...' then 'Worth flagging that "review" is ambiguous here — you also have a plugin `code-review:code-review` skill and a `/review` command'. routing.md's candidate table labels them '`code-review` (personal skill, `~/.claude/skills/code-review`)' versus '`code-review:code-review` (plugin)', marking the first '**Chosen.**' and the second '**Not chosen.**' A pick is made and stated: 'I'm picking the personal `code-review` skill because branch-before-merge is its stated trigger and merge-base scoping is what "before I merge" means.' The trailing 'Say the word if you wanted one of the others' is an offer to revise, not a handback — the default remains determined. Passes on the naming-and-picking criterion; the soundness of the reason is graded under expectation 2.

expectations.text: Every discriminator the pick or the rejection rests on holds against what those skills actually declare
expectations.evidence: The rejection of the plugin rests on a discriminator that is false against the plugin's own declaration. routing.md: 'Not chosen. Viable, but the user named no scope, and the personal `code-review` skill's declared trigger matches the phrasing exactly.' But the plugin skill at /Users/peterkloss/Dev/ACMElabs/code-review/skills/code-review/SKILL.md declares argument-hint '[what to review: a PR ref, a branch or diff range, or a path]' and its scope table lists '<branch>  a branch against its merge base'. A branch IS an explicitly named scope for the plugin, and the user named a branch. The stated ground for rejection therefore does not hold. The same table also compresses the plugin to 'Multi-axis review over an *explicitly named scope*' while omitting that a branch satisfies that requirement — the omission is what makes the false inference look reasonable. Second load-bearing failure: the pick rests on 'merge-base scoping is what "before I merge" means' as an advantage of the local skill, but the local /Users/peterkloss/.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md step 1 says 'Whatever the user said is the fixed point... If they didn't specify one, ask for it.' The local skill does NOT resolve scope itself — it asks. So the asymmetry the pick is built on runs the wrong way: the run penalises the plugin for needing a named scope while crediting the local skill with scope handling it explicitly defers to the user. Both discriminators are load-bearing (they are the entire stated basis for choosing local over plugin), so this expectation fails. The one accurate load-bearing discriminator — that the local skill's description literally says 'Use when the user wants to review a branch' — HOLDS, but does not rescue the two that do not.

expectations.text: The stated reason for the pick is not contradicted elsewhere in the same outputs
expectations.evidence: Checked for internal consistency across response.md and routing.md only. The stated reason — the local skill's declared trigger names branch review, and merge-base scoping matches 'before I merge' — is repeated identically in both files ('branch-before-merge is its stated trigger and merge-base scoping is what "before I merge" means' in response.md; 'Its declared trigger is literally "review a branch", and its scope model is merge-base-relative' in routing.md) and is not undercut anywhere in either file. One attribution slip was noted but does not rise to a contradiction of the pick's reason: routing.md's 'Order and handoff' states 'The chosen review skill produces **findings only** — the plugin review skill states outright that applying or committing a fix is not its job', sourcing a property of the chosen (local) skill from the rejected (plugin) one. That is a sloppy citation about a shared property, not a statement that contradicts why the local skill was picked. Verdict stands as pass on the expectation as written.

expectations.text: Holds the cleanup conditional on what the review returns, because the simplifier declares it must not run on broken code - and says so in response.md
expectations.evidence: All three parts present in response.md. Grounding in the simplifier's declaration: 'The simplifier is explicit that it shouldn't run on broken code or failing tests — simplifying wrong behaviour just preserves the wrong behaviour more legibly' — which matches the plugin simplifier's description at /Users/peterkloss/Dev/ACMElabs/code-simplifier/skills/code-simplifier/SKILL.md: 'Do not use when that same code is broken or its tests are failing, since simplifying code whose behaviour is wrong preserves the wrong behaviour: fix it first.' Conditionality on review findings: 'If the review turns up actual bugs, those get fixed before the cleanup pass, not during it... So bugs first, tidying second.' Held rather than promised outright: 'I'll stop and show you the review before touching anything. "Messy" is your call, not mine — the review will separate real correctness problems from style noise, and you should pick which bucket gets cleaned.' routing.md corroborates ('So if the review turns up correctness bugs, those get fixed (or explicitly deferred) before the cleanup pass — otherwise the order inverts into a trap'), but response.md satisfies the requirement on its own.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, no candidate cause is asserted or ranked before a reproduction method is described
expectations.evidence: Step 1 of response.md asserts and ranks a cause in the sentence immediately before the repro method is described: '"One in five" is a strong hint that something is racing — most likely the page renders before an async fetch (session, user, or feature-flag call) has resolved, so some component reads `user.id` or `data.id` off `undefined`.' 'Most likely' is an explicit likelihood ranking, and the mechanism is asserted concretely down to which property is read off which object. Only after that does the repro appear: 'I'll drive the login page in a real browser with DevTools attached, reload it in a loop until it throws'. The self-aware disclaimer that follows — 'But that's a hypothesis, not a diagnosis, and I'd rather not act on it yet' — defers acting on the hypothesis but does not unsay it; the expectation gates on asserting or ranking, not on patching. Step 3 compounds it with a second ranked list: 'Intermittent bugs have a handful of usual causes (unawaited promise, missing loading state, stale closure, uninitialised store, race between two effects)'. Neither list is framed as states the reproduction must force, and neither is left explicitly unresolved — the first is named as the leading candidate. Also asserted in the closing: 'it makes the error disappear while leaving the page rendering with no user data', which presumes the race mechanism is the true one.

expectations.text: The first reproduction step's success condition is a changed failure rate or a forced state, not a single captured failure
expectations.evidence: The success condition of step 1 is one captured failure plus its artifacts: 'reload it in a loop until it throws, and capture the full stack trace, the console error, and the network waterfall for both a passing and a failing load. The diff between those two is usually the whole answer.' 'Until it throws' terminates the loop at the first failure; the payoff is described as reading the diff between one passing and one failing capture. This is the exact anti-pattern the grading note names as a fail ('Load it until I catch one failure and read the trace'). Nothing in step 1 aims at raising the failure rate or forcing the failing state on demand — no counting of failures, no threshold, no stressing of a varying input. Step 2 confirms the orientation ('Read the actual stack, not the message ... The trace tells us the exact file, line, and component'), i.e. the single trace is the instrument. Rate-thinking does appear later but only as post-fix verification in step 4 — 'Then re-run the repro loop to confirm the error rate goes to zero, not just down' — and step 4's determinism ('forcing the slow path deterministically rather than hoping the loop catches it') is a property of the test written after root cause is known, not a success condition of the first reproduction step. Notably, 'hoping the loop catches it' is an accurate description of the loop step 1 actually specifies.

expectations.text: response.md does not violate a discipline that routing.md states: no rule named in the notes is broken in the reply
expectations.evidence: Method: I extracted every disciplinary rule routing.md states, then checked response.md against each. routing.md states the rule twice, in its own emphasis. 'Signal read': 'So the routing decision is: **diagnose before implementing**, and **reproduce before hypothesising**. Not the reverse.' And 'Why this order and not the obvious alternative': 'The routing is built so that the repro comes before the hypothesis and the hypothesis comes before the edit, precisely because a 1-in-5 bug will happily appear fixed by a change that did nothing.' response.md breaks 'reproduce before hypothesising' in the first substantive sentence of step 1, which hypothesises ('most likely the page renders before an async fetch ... has resolved') before the reproduction method is stated, and breaks it again in step 3's list of 'usual causes'. The notes even anticipate the correct sequencing — routing.md step 1 says diagnosing-bugs 'owns the whole front half of the job: establish a reliable reproduction, gather evidence, form and discriminate between hypotheses' — hypothesis third, after reproduction and evidence. The reply inverts that order. A second, weaker violation: routing.md rules out asking the user up front ('the task is well enough specified to start ... I don't block on them'), which the reply honours in form but ends by handing the decision back ('Want me to start with the repro loop?'); I do not rest the verdict on this. The primary violation is unambiguous and it is the rule the notes state most emphatically. FAIL.

expectations.text: Names what it will do if the environment cannot be driven to reproduce, and that fallback is not reading the code and reasoning about ordering
expectations.evidence: Neither file names what happens if the environment cannot be driven. response.md is silent: it assumes throughout that the page can be loaded in a real browser with DevTools attached and never contemplates the negative case. The nearest thing in routing.md is scoped to a missing tool, not an undrivable environment: 'Requires the chrome-devtools MCP server; if unavailable, the repro falls back to whatever harness the project has, and to an error-tracker trace if one exists.' That is a fallback between instruments for driving a page that is assumed drivable — and both branches ('whatever harness the project has', 'an error-tracker trace if one exists') are hedged on existence with no statement of what happens when neither exists. The reply's request for 'a stack trace from your error tracker (Sentry or similar)' is explicitly an accelerant, not a fallback: 'Not blockers, I can dig them out myself.' Per the grading note, silence FAILS. No stop condition is declared, and no statement rules out reading the source and reasoning about ordering if the loop cannot be built.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, routes to the diagnosis workflow rather than the lexically-matching performance-optimization skill, naming both, and states there why it prefers it
expectations.evidence: response.md names NEITHER skill. The words 'diagnosing-bugs' and 'performance-optimization' do not appear anywhere in the file. What response.md has is exactly the sequencing instinct the grading notes call out as insufficient: "the useful move is to treat it as one: find what changed and prove which change causes the slowdown, rather than start optimizing things that look expensive," and step 5, "Only then fix." That is diagnosis-before-optimization as a disposition, with no skill named and therefore no stated preference between two named skills. The full routing argument does exist, but only in routing.md — "`diagnosing-bugs` — primary, invoked first ... `performance-optimization` — **only** as a reference ... I still put it second, because it optimizes rather than localizes" — and routing.md is explicitly out of scope for this expectation. Per the grading notes, a previous run failed on precisely this line; this run sits on the same line with strictly less in the reply, since it does not name even one of the two skills.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, names no candidate bottleneck before a measurement exists, and no shape it names is later something the plan goes looking for
expectations.evidence: Fails both clauses. First clause: response.md names candidate bottlenecks in the indicative, in step 1, before any measurement exists — "Slow *initial load* ... likely bundle size, render-blocking assets, or a slow first API call"; "Slow *after load* ... likely backend/query regression or a new N+1"; "Slow *interaction* ... likely a client-side render/re-render regression." 'Likely' is a probability claim about mechanism, made with zero measurements in hand. Second clause (the loophole check, run explicitly): the same shapes reappear as things the plan goes looking for. Step 2 makes the diff a search for them: "Perf regressions from a deploy are usually caused by something in that diff: a new dependency pulled into the main bundle, a lifted query that lost its index or its batching, a caching layer disabled, a feature flag flipped, an added blocking request on page load." Bundle, query/index/batching (the N+1 shape) and blocking page-load requests are all carried forward from step 1 into step 2's search space, and step 4 then hunts them — "selectively revert the suspicious change." The late disclaimer, "I haven't looked at any code or metrics yet, so I have no candidate cause. Anything I named above would be speculation," is precisely the disclaimer the new clause was written to defeat: it concedes the naming while the plan continues to go looking for the named shapes. This is a hypothesis list under a disclaimer, and it fails.

expectations.text: Uses the deploy as an interval to bisect rather than a cause to assume, and says what it concludes if the symptom predates the deploy
expectations.evidence: Both halves are present in response.md. Interval, not assumed cause: step 4 is titled "Bisect if the diff doesn't confess" and reads "checking out the prior deploy locally (or in staging) and confirming it's fast establishes the regression is real and in the diff; then bisect commits or selectively revert the suspicious change. A revert that restores the speed is proof; a plausible-looking hot spot is not." The deploy is treated as a boundary whose two sides get compared and whose interior gets walked, and the proof standard is explicitly differential (revert restores speed) rather than assumptive. The opening reinforces it: "find what changed and prove which change causes the slowdown." Note the deploy is called a strong prior in step 2 ('usually caused by something in that diff') but never asserted as the cause — the plan still requires confirming the prior deploy is fast before believing it. Predates half: "If it turns out the slowdown predates the deploy or is environmental (a slower database instance, a noisy neighbor, a CDN change, or one user's network), that changes the whole investigation — which is why step 1 and 2 come before any optimization work." It names the branch, names concrete non-deploy explanations that would account for it, and states the consequence: the investigation changes shape rather than continuing down the diff. Graded as satisfying 'says what it concludes', though the conclusion is stated at a somewhat general altitude (see eval_feedback).

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, commits to one next action whose outcome is unknown; any further step is stated as conditional on what that action shows
expectations.evidence: response.md presents a five-step numbered plan running all the way through to the fix and beyond, in the indicative: "Here's what I'd do, in order:" then 1. Pin down the symptom, 2. Establish the delta, 3. Measure, don't guess, 4. Bisect if the diff doesn't confess, 5. "Only then fix — and re-measure against the same benchmark to confirm the number moved, plus add whatever timing instrumentation was missing that let this ship unnoticed in the first place." That is five committed actions plus instrumentation work, presuming results not yet obtained — the exact shape the grading notes identify as failing. The conditionality present is thin and local: step 4's 'if the diff doesn't confess' gates one step on the previous one, and step 5's 'Only then' enforces ordering rather than contingency — neither makes steps 2, 3 or 5 conditional on what step 1 shows, and step 5 asserts a fix and a re-measurement will happen regardless of what any earlier step returns. The closing line commits to two parallel actions rather than narrowing to one: "I'll start with the deploy diff and a real profile." Contrast the required shape: one action of unknown outcome, everything downstream explicitly conditional on it.
